On the last day of June, the city auctioned off everything that had been left on a bus.

There were forty-six umbrellas, a trombone, a slow cooker with the lid taped on, and a framed photograph of a woman standing beside a hole in the ground. The auctioneer held up the photograph.

“Any information on the hole?” someone asked.

The auctioneer turned it over. “West-facing, apparently.”

I had come for my father’s toolbox. He’d left it on the number nine eleven months earlier, and every Tuesday since, he’d called the depot and asked if it had turned up. When they finally said yes, he said they could keep it.

“You called them forty-seven times,” I said.

“Forty-eight,” he said. “I called twice on my birthday.”

I bought the toolbox for six dollars. On the bus home I opened it and found, in the little tray where the drill bits went, a house key with a paper tag: *For when you stop knocking.*

I’d been knocking at my father’s door every Sunday for nine years. He always took his time answering. Sometimes, if the window was open, I could hear him turn down the radio and set his mug in the sink. Then came the scrape of his chair.

That Sunday I let myself in.

“Did you get a receipt?” he called from the kitchen.

I put it on the table. He read it carefully, folded it in half, and tucked it into the toolbox.

“Six dollars,” he said. “They saw you coming.”

The kettle was already on.
